paragraphs.text: Mitchell-Riley syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder. Its cardinal features are neonatal diabetes, hypoplastic or annular pancreas, duodenal and jejunal atresia, and aplasia or hypoplasia of the gallbladder (Mitchell et al., 2004). Affected infants also have intractable diarrhea that does not respond to pancreatic enzyme replacement. Pancreatic islets lack cells staining for insulin, glucagon, or somatostatin (Smith et al., 2010). In a review of molecularly confirmed cases, Sansbury et al. (2015) found duodenal atresia in all patients, gallbladder agenesis and intrahepatic cholestasis in most, and death within the first year in more than half. They also described patients with childhood-onset diabetes who survived longer.

paragraphs.text: Mitchell et al. (2004) described 5 infants from 3 families: 2 sib pairs and 1 isolated case. One sib pair was born to consanguineous parents. The infants had neonatal diabetes, hypoplastic or annular pancreas, jejunal atresia, duodenal atresia, and aplasia or hypoplasia of the gallbladder. Four of the children died in the first year of life despite aggressive medical management. One patient with a milder form was surviving without insulin. Pancreatic immunohistochemistry in 3 of the infants showed a few scattered chromogranin A-positive cell clusters but no insulin, glucagon, or somatostatin staining at all. Exocrine histology varied between cases.

paragraphs.text: Sansbury et al. (2015) reported 2 Turkish double first cousins. The parents were not consanguineous, but the mothers were sisters and the fathers were brothers. Case 1 was a girl born at 32 weeks' gestation (birth weight 1.65 kg) with duodenal atresia, a jejunal web, and Meckel diverticulum. Hyperglycemia was noted at age 2 years. At 3 years she presented with diabetic ketoacidosis, very low insulin and C-peptide, and negative islet autoantibodies, and she was treated with insulin. She had recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding due to gastric heterotopia in the small bowel, which resolved after resection at age 5. She also had an absent gallbladder with normal liver function. Her identical twin had duodenal atresia and died at 1 month. Case 2, her male cousin, was born at 34 weeks (birth weight 1.70 kg) with duodenal atresia and midgut malrotation. He had asymptomatic fasting hyperglycemia at age 5 and was diagnosed with diabetes at age 6 years, with undetectable insulin, low C-peptide, and negative autoantibodies. He required insulin. He had chronic iron deficiency anemia of unknown cause and no hepatobiliary abnormality.

paragraphs.text: Sansbury et al. (2015) also reviewed 8 previously published molecularly confirmed cases of Mitchell-Riley syndrome. All 8 had duodenal atresia, with or without jejunal atresia or midgut malrotation. Seven of 8 had gallbladder agenesis, 7 of 8 had intrahepatic cholestasis, and another had ascites. Five of 8 died within the first year. Compared with these cases, the authors' 2 new patients had childhood-onset diabetes, no liver pathology, and longer survival.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2010) showed in mice that Rfx6 acts downstream of Neurog3. After gastrulation, Rfx6 is expressed broadly in definitive endoderm. Its expression then becomes restricted to the gut and pancreatic bud, is reactivated by Neurog3 in islet progenitor cells, and is finally restricted to the islets. The authors noted that NEUROG3 mutations also cause intractable diarrhea and diabetes, but not small bowel atresia or biliary abnormalities. They attributed this difference to Rfx6 expression in early gut endoderm, where Neurog3 is not expressed. Using EMSA, Smith et al. (2010) showed that Rfx6 and Rfx3 form a heterodimeric complex that binds an X box site. The 2 factors cooperated in activating a promoter containing multimers of this site. The authors concluded that Rfx3 and Rfx6 cooperate in regulating genes involved in islet development but not in cilia formation.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2010) generated Rfx6-null mice by replacing the first 5 exons with an eGFP-cre cassette. Homozygous mice were born at the expected mendelian ratio. However, they did not feed normally, had gross bowel distension due to small bowel obstruction, and died within 2 days of birth. Some had reduced pancreas size. At embryonic day 17.5, mutant pancreata contained many chromogranin A-positive endocrine cells, but none expressed insulin, glucagon, somatostatin, or ghrelin. Cells expressing pancreatic polypeptide were increased. Neurog3 expression was unaffected in the mutant pancreata. Expression was reduced for the alpha-cell factors Irx2 and Arx and for the insulin transcription factors Pax6, MafA, NeuroD1, and Pdx1. Nkx2.2 and Nkx6.1 levels were not significantly changed, Pax4 was increased, and Nkx6.1 expression expanded to all endocrine cells. Primary cilia formed normally, in contrast to Rfx3-null mice.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2010) studied proband 2, the offspring of second cousins, who had Mitchell-Riley syndrome and was alive at age 4.5 years. Array capture and deep sequencing of the shared homozygous regions identified a homozygous ser217-to-pro (S217P) substitution in the RFX6 gene. This was the only nonsynonymous variant among 30 novel variants detected, and direct sequencing confirmed it. The mutation was inherited from carrier parents. S217P lies between the DNA-binding and dimerization domains. It only modestly reduced DNA binding and did not affect dimer formation.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2010) studied proband 3, who had Mitchell-Riley syndrome and was alive at age 9 years, intermittently off insulin. This patient was compound heterozygous for 2 splice mutations in the RFX6 gene. The first was a T-to-G transversion at position +2 of intron 6 (IVS6+2T-G), which abolished the splice donor site. The second was an A-to-G transition at position -12 of intron 1 (IVS1-12A-G), which disrupted the splice acceptor site. Both mutations were inherited from carrier parents.

paragraphs.text: Sansbury et al. (2015) studied 2 Turkish double first cousins with Mitchell-Riley syndrome and childhood-onset diabetes. Both carried a c.2596C-T transition in exon 18 of the RFX6 gene, resulting in an arg866-to-ter (R866X) substitution. The mutation occurred in compound heterozygosity with R726X and was inherited from the mothers. Because R866X lies within 50 nucleotides of the last exon-exon boundary, the authors predicted that it escapes nonsense-mediated decay. The result would be a partially truncated protein with a preserved DNA-binding domain that might retain some function. They suggested this could explain the milder phenotype, with later-onset diabetes and no liver pathology.
